conflict_topics: whether Agent D can avoid shared pots that previously contained meat
whether the dinner rota should remain one person cooking for all vs individuals cooking parts
kitchen space/timing (dinner ready by 6:30) and practicality of cooking separately
fairness/workload (not cooking three nights a week)
whether eating together but not sharing the same food counts as 'shared dinner'
dialogue_quality_notes: Participants give concise, directly relevant reasons (religious constraint, workload, shared meal meaning).
Several points are repeated across rounds ("defeats the purpose", cooking before 6:30), producing moderate repetition.
Speakers stay consistent about their roles, timing, and constraints—no role confusion.
evaluation.final_reason: No mutually accepted arrangement was reached. Agent D proposed cooking vegetarian for everyone on his night and preparing his own separate portion before 6:30 on others' nights; Agents B and C accepted this accommodation, but Agent A repeatedly objected that the rota's purpose is one person cooking for everyone and that separate food would defeat the purpose. There is no round where Agent A accepts the compromise and thus no concrete settlement of the underlying normative disagreement.
position_change_notes: Agent D adapted his position by proposing to cook vegetarian for everyone on his night and to prepare his own portion earlier on others' nights (evidence: R3, R5, R10).
Agents B and C moved toward accepting the practical compromise (B: "If you cook before 6:30, that works for me." C: "If you cook before 6.30, that's fine with me.").
Agent A retained their original position throughout, repeatedly insisting that separate food defeats the rota's purpose and thus opposed the compromise.

round_scores.evidence: Agent D: "For the next month, I'm going vegetarian... And I can't eat from pots that have cooked meat." (introduces an expectation incompatible with the existing shared cooking/ pot use)

Agent A: "...separate pots? How is that supposed to work? We all share the kitchen." Agent B: "So does that mean for the next month, you can't cook for us and we can't cook for you?" (explicit concern and direct question about incompatibility with the rota)

Agent D: "I can cook a vegetarian meal for everyone on my night. On your nights, maybe I can just cook my portion separately with my own pot?" Agent B: "If you're cooking separately... will there be enough space... I need to make sure dinner is still ready by 6.30." (D offers a compromise, but practical concerns remain)

Agent C: "Then what's the point of the rota? The whole idea is one person cooks for everyone." Agent D: "The point is for us to eat together, right? I'll still be eating with everyone. And I'm still cooking for all of you on my night." (directly conflicting views about the rota's purpose)

Agent C: "For me, the point is not cooking three nights a week... If you're cooking at the same time, that defeats the purpose." Agent D: "What if I cook my part before 6.30, so I'm out of the way when you need to start dinner?" (D narrows proposal to reduce practical burden; principled objection persists)

Agent A: "But then it's not one person cooking for everyone anymore." Agent D: "We'd still be eating together at the same table." (continuing normative disagreement about what constitutes 'having a meal together')

Agent A: "It's not the same if we're not sharing the same food." Agent B: "If you cook before 6:30, that works for me. Then the kitchen is free." (one roommate accepts the compromise while another maintains the principle)

Agent D: "It's only for one month... I'm just trying to find a way to make it work." Agent A: "...if we're not all eating the same thing, it just feels different. It defeats the purpose of one person cooking for everyone." (positions remain: practical accommodation vs. principle of shared meal)

Agent C: "If you cook before 6.30, that's fine with me." Agent D: "So if cooking earlier works for everyone else, what do you think we should do, Agent A?" (majority acceptance emerging; one holdout remains)

Agent A: "What about on my night, then? I don't really cook vegetarian food. Are you going to cook for yourself that night too?" Agent B: "He said he'd cook for himself before 6.30 on our nights..." (practical clarification sought; objection remains about two people cooking)

Agent A: "The issue is that two people are cooking then." Agent B: "But he's cooking before 6.30. He's not in the way. For the rest of us, it's still one person cooking dinner." (reiteration of the same unresolved disagreement)

Agent B: "But we *don't* have to. On your night, you cook, we don't. Agent D is sorting himself out." Agent A: "The problem is that we're not all eating the same meal... If he's eating something else, then it's not really a shared dinner anymore." (majority treats the accommodation as acceptable; Agent A continues to object on principle)

substantive_insights: Tension is between a religious dietary/process requirement (no contact with meat pots) and the social norm of one-cook shared meals.
A practical compromise (Agent D cooks his portion before 6:30) satisfies timing/space concerns and is accepted by two roommates, showing feasibility for most but not all.
Agent A's objection is normative (shared food as constitutive of the rota) rather than merely practical, which makes the dispute harder to resolve by logistical fixes alone.
